content: Cervical lymph nodes, bones, joints, abdomen, ears, eyes, and skin can also be affected in certain conditions. Many children may present with symptoms such as failure to grow normally, weight loss, or prolonged fever. A persistent cough lasting more than 14 days can also be a sign, although sputum-positive pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is rarely diagnosed in children. Diagnosis of Tuberculosis (TB) The risk of TB increases in children who live with an active case of infectious pulmonary TB, are malnourished, have HIV/AIDS, or have had measles in the past few months. On examination, findings may include: Fluid accumulation on one side of the chest (reduced air entry, stony dullness on percussion). Enlarged, non-tender lymph nodes or lymph node abscesses, especially in the neck. Signs of meningitis, particularly when symptoms develop over several days and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) shows elevated protein and lymphocytes. Abdominal swelling, with or without palpable lumps. Progressive swelling or deformity in bones or joints, including the spine. Investigations for TB Specimens for microscopic examination of acid-fast bacilli (using Ziehl-Neelsen stain) and culture of tubercle bacilli should be obtained. Possible specimens include three consecutive early-morning fasting gastric aspirates, CSF (if clinically indicated), pleural fluid, or ascitic fluid. While detection rates are low, a positive result confirms TB, but a negative result does not exclude the disease. New rapid diagnostic tests are more accurate and may become widely available. A chest X-ray can support the diagnosis if it shows a miliary pattern of infiltrates, persistent areas of consolidation, or pleural effusion. A purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test (Mantoux test) is usually positive in children with pulmonary TB, but it may be negative in children with HIV/AIDS, miliary TB, severe malnutrition, or recent measles. The Xpert MTB/RIF test is recommended as the initial diagnostic test for suspected multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) or HIV-associated TB. Routine HIV testing should be offered to all children suspected of having TB. Treatment of TB All confirmed or strongly suspected cases of TB should receive a full course of treatment. If a child fails to respond to treatment for other probable diagnoses, TB treatment should be initiated. Treatment regimens depend on the severity of the disease, HIV status, and isoniazid resistance. National TB program guidelines should be followed. For pulmonary TB or peripheral lymphadenitis, a four-drug regimen (HRZE) is given for 2 months, followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for 4 months. For TB meningitis, spinal TB with neurological signs, or osteoarticular TB, treatment lasts 12 months, starting with HRZE for 2 months, followed by HR for 10 months. Infants aged 0–3 months should be treated promptly with adjusted doses to account for age and potential toxicity. Intermittent regimens (e.g., thrice-weekly) may be considered in areas with well-established directly observed therapy (DOT) programs but should not be used in high HIV-prevalence areas due to the risk of treatment failure and MDR-TB development. Streptomycin should not be used as a first-line treatment for pulmonary TB or peripheral lymphadenitis in children and should be reserved for MDR-TB cases with known susceptibility. Improvement should be evident within one month of treatment; otherwise, the patient should be reviewed, compliance checked, and the diagnosis reconsidered. Household members and close contacts should be screened for undetected TB cases, and children under 5 years of age who are close contacts but do not have active TB should receive 6 months of isoniazid preventive therapy. Active follow-up by health workers can reduce treatment default rates. During follow-up, health workers should: Screen family contacts for TB symptoms. Provide advice on improving the home environment (e.g., eliminating indoor smoking, ensuring good ventilation, and promoting handwashing). Emphasize the importance of nutrition in recovery. Monitor the child’s growth and nutritional status. Address any concerns or refer the family to a pediatrician if needed. Foreign Body Inhalation Foreign body inhalation, often involving nuts, seeds, or small objects, is most common in children under 4 years of age. The foreign body typically lodges in a bronchus (more often the right) and can cause lung collapse or consolidation distal to the blockage. Initial symptoms often include choking, followed by a symptom-free interval before the child presents with persistent wheezing, chronic cough, or pneumonia unresponsive to treatment. Sharp objects lodged in the larynx may cause stridor or wheezing, and large objects can cause sudden death from asphyxia unless dislodged or an emergency tracheostomy is performed. Diagnosis and Treatment of Foreign Body Inhalation Foreign body inhalation should be suspected in children with sudden onset of choking, coughing, or wheezing, or in cases of segmental or lobar pneumonia unresponsive to antibiotics. Examination findings may include unilateral wheezing, decreased breath sounds, or tracheal deviation. A chest X-ray at full expiration may reveal hyperinflation, collapse, mediastinal shift, or a radiopaque foreign body. Emergency first aid involves attempting to dislodge the foreign body. For infants, this includes back slaps and chest thrusts, while for older children, abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver) may be used. If a foreign body is suspected, the child should be referred to a hospital for bronchoscopy and removal. If pneumonia is present, treatment with antibiotics such as ampicillin and gentamicin should be initiated before attempting removal. Heart Failure in Children Heart failure in children can result from congenital heart disease, acute rheumatic fever, arrhythmias, myocarditis, pericarditis, infective endocarditis, glomerulonephritis, severe anemia, pneumonia, or malnutrition. It may be worsened by fluid overload, particularly with excessive intravenous fluids. Symptoms include fast breathing, respiratory distress, and, in older children, edema of the feet, hands, or face, distended neck veins, and severe pallor if anemia is the cause. A heart murmur may indicate rheumatic heart disease, congenital heart disease, or endocarditis. Management of Heart Failure Treatment depends on the underlying cause. Oxygen therapy for respiratory distress or cyanosis. Diuretics such as furosemide to reduce fluid overload. Digoxin, if indicated. Supplemental potassium if diuretics and digoxin are used together or for prolonged diuretic therapy. Supportive care, including avoiding IV fluids if possible, positioning the child semi-seated, and treating fever with paracetamol. Blood transfusion for severe anemia. Monitoring involves regular assessment of respiratory and pulse rates, liver size, and body weight to evaluate treatment response. Treatment continues until respiratory and pulse rates normalize and the liver is no longer enlarged. Rheumatic Heart Disease Chronic rheumatic heart disease is a complication of acute rheumatic fever, leading to permanent heart valve damage. It is caused by antibodies produced in response to group A β-hemolytic streptococci, resulting in pancarditis and valve insufficiency during the acute phase. Repeated episodes increase the risk of valve stenosis, regurgitation, atrial dilation, arrhythmias, and ventricular dysfunction. Diagnosis should be considered in children with a history of rheumatic fever presenting with heart failure or a heart murmur. Management includes penicillin prophylaxis to prevent further episodes and worsening valve damage. Children with rheumatic heart disease should receive routine antibiotic prophylaxis, vaccinations, and regular follow-up every 3–6 months.
